CausalChain: Excess lipid accumulation in NAFLD -> Increased ROS production and lipid peroxidation -> Generation of reactive aldehydes (e.g., 4-HNE) -> Lysosomal membrane destabilization -> Enhanced NCOA4-mediated ferritinophagy -> Increased labile iron pool -> Amplified Fenton reaction -> Further lipid peroxidation -> Exacerbated ferroptosis
Hypothesis: In hepatocytes undergoing metabolic stress, accumulation of 4-HNE leads to lysosomal membrane destabilization that accelerates NCOA4-driven ferritinophagy, establishing a feed-forward loop that increases intracellular free iron and exacerbates ferroptosis, thereby promoting the progression from NAFLD to NASH.
Abstract: Hepatic diseases such as non‐alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) are often characterized by an accumulation of lipids and iron, conditions that predispose hepatocytes to oxidative stress and cell death. In this study, we propose a novel mechanistic hypothesis in which the accumulation of lipid peroxidation products, notably 4‐hydroxy-nonenal (4-HNE), compromises lysosomal membrane integrity. This lysosomal destabilization then triggers an enhanced NCOA4-mediated ferritin degradation (ferritinophagy), which increases the labile iron pool and amplifies the Fenton reaction, thereby exacerbating lipid peroxidation and culminating in ferroptotic cell death. This feed-forward loop may critically drive the progression from simple steatosis to non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) and eventually to liver fibrosis. Pharmacological interventions aimed at stabilizing lysosomal membranes or modulating ferritinophagy could, therefore, represent promising therapeutic strategies to mitigate ferroptosis-driven liver injury.
